questions.question: A spinner is divided into 8 equal sections. 3 sections are red and the other 5 sections are white. The spinner is spun once. What is the theoretical probability of landing on red?
questions.explain: List all the equally likely outcomes first: 8 equal sections in the whole spinner, and 3 of them are red, so P(red) = 3/8. The common trap is writing 3/5, which compares red parts to white parts instead of red parts to the whole spinner.

questions.question: A spinner has 10 equal sections. 5 sections are red, 3 sections are blue, and 2 sections are yellow. The spinner is spun once. What is the theoretical probability of landing on blue?
questions.explain: The 10 equal sections are the equally likely outcomes, and 3 of them are blue, so P(blue) = 3/10. Do not answer 1/3 just because there are three colours: the colours cover different numbers of sections, so they are not equally likely.

questions.question: A spinner is divided into 12 equal sections, numbered 1 to 12, with each number used exactly once. The spinner is spun one time. What is the theoretical probability of landing on 7?
questions.explain: There are 12 equally likely outcomes (the numbers 1 to 12) and only one of them is 7, so P(7) = 1/12. The trap is thinking it is 1/2 because you either get 7 or you do not: those two results are not equally likely.

questions.question: A prize spinner at a school fun fair has 5 equal sections. 4 sections say Prize and 1 section says Try again. The spinner is spun once. What is the theoretical probability of landing on Try again?
questions.explain: Count all the equal sections as outcomes: there are 5, and 1 says Try again, so P(Try again) = 1/5. The one that says 1/4 compares the Try again section to the 4 Prize sections instead of to the whole spinner of 5.

questions.question: Eight cards are placed face down. They are labelled 2, 2, 4, 6, 6, 6, 9, 9. One card is picked without looking. What is the theoretical probability of picking a 6?
questions.explain: Each card is one equally likely outcome, so there are 8 outcomes and three of them are 6, giving P(6) = 3/8. Answering 1/4 treats the four different numbers 2, 4, 6 and 9 as equally likely, but 6 appears on more cards than the others.

questions.question: Ana makes one letter tile for each letter in the word VICTORIA, so she has 8 tiles: V, I, C, T, O, R, I, A. She turns them face down, mixes them, and picks one tile. What is the theoretical probability of picking the letter I?
questions.explain: There are 8 tiles, so 8 equally likely outcomes, and the letter I is on 2 of them, so P(I) = 2/8, which is 1/4. The trap is answering 1/8 by counting the letter I only once, or 1/7 by counting only the 7 different letters.

questions.question: A community centre sells 25 raffle tickets for a $20 gift card, and each ticket has an equal chance of being drawn. Maya buys 4 of the tickets. What is the theoretical probability that Maya's ticket is the one drawn?
questions.explain: All 25 tickets are equally likely outcomes and 4 of them belong to Maya, so P(Maya wins) = 4/25. Answering 4/21 compares Maya's tickets to everyone else's tickets instead of to all 25 tickets.

questions.question: A jar in a Nanaimo classroom holds 11 marbles: 5 green, 4 orange, and 2 purple. One marble is drawn without looking. What is the theoretical probability of drawing an orange marble?
questions.explain: Each marble is one equally likely outcome, so there are 11 outcomes and 4 of them are orange: P(orange) = 4/11. The 4/7 compares the orange marbles with the 7 that are not orange instead of with the whole jar, 1/3 wrongly treats the three colours as equally likely even though they have different counts, and 1/11 counts orange as if it were a single marble.

questions.question: Sofia's spinner has 4 equal sections coloured red, blue, yellow, and green. She spins it 20 times and lands on red 8 times. Before her next spin, what is the theoretical probability of landing on red?
questions.explain: Theoretical probability comes from listing the equally likely outcomes, not from what happened in the trials: there are 4 equal sections and 1 is red, so P(red) = 1/4. The result 8 out of 20 is the experimental probability, so the one that says 2/5 answers a different question.

questions.question: A snack bin at an after-school program holds 6 granola bars, 4 packs of apple slices, and 2 boxes of raisins. Before snack time the leader adds 4 more granola bars to the bin. A student then reaches in and takes one snack without looking. What is the theoretical probability of taking a box of raisins?
questions.explain: Update the total first: 6 + 4 + 4 = 14 granola bars and apple packs plus 2 raisin boxes gives 16 snacks in all, so P(raisins) = 2/16, which is 1/8. The trap is using the old total of 12 and answering 2/12, or comparing 2 raisin boxes to the 14 other snacks.

questions.question: A charity spinner at a school fair has 10 equal sections: 1 section says Win $5, 3 sections say Win $2, and 6 sections say Thanks for playing. Ravi says the probability of winning $5 is 1/3 because there are three different results on the spinner. What is the correct theoretical probability of winning $5?
questions.explain: The equally likely outcomes are the 10 equal sections, not the 3 kinds of results, and only 1 section says Win $5, so P(Win $5) = 1/10. Ravi's 1/3 assumes three unequal results happen equally often, and 1/9 compares the winning section to the other 9 instead of to all 10.

questions.question: A draw box at a Burnaby rec centre camp holds 30 name sticks: 12 from Grade 4, 10 from Grade 5, and 8 from Grade 6. Just before the draw, 5 of the Grade 4 sticks are taken out because those campers went home early. One stick is then drawn without looking. What is the theoretical probability of drawing a Grade 6 name?
questions.explain: Update the total first: 30 − 5 = 25 sticks stay in the box, and 8 of them are Grade 6, so P(Grade 6) = 8/25. The 8/30 uses the old total from before the sticks were removed, 1/3 pretends the three grades hold equal numbers of sticks, and 8/17 compares the Grade 6 sticks with the 17 other sticks instead of with all 25.
